memory.abstract: Ewald message passing introduces a Fourier-space long-range interaction scheme for molecular GNNs, using frequency cutoffs instead of distance cutoffs to capture electrostatics and van der Waals forces, achieving 10-16% energy MAE improvements on OC20 and OE62 datasets.

content.background: Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) have become dominant for learning molecular properties from quantum chemical data, achieving orders of magnitude speedup over DFT while preserving accuracy. However, MPNNs fundamentally rely on distance cutoffs for computational efficiency, which creates a critical limitation: they cannot capture long-range physical interactions such as electrostatics and van der Waals forces that decay as power laws (e.g., 1/r for electrostatics). This is particularly problematic for periodic systems (materials) where interatomic distances are unbounded, and for large molecules where remote atom interactions contribute significantly to target properties. The distance cutoff truncation induces severe artifacts in thermochemical predictions even at large cutoffs. In classical molecular dynamics, this problem is solved via Ewald summation, which decomposes interactions into a short-range part (fast decay in distance, truncated in real space) and a long-range part (slow decay in distance but fast decay in Fourier space, truncated in frequency space). This work bridges Ewald summation and MPNNs by proposing Ewald message passing as a general framework to complement existing GNN layers.
content.method: The core insight is the formal correspondence between electrostatic potentials and continuous-filter convolutions in MPNNs. In electrostatics, the potential V_i(x_i) = Σ_j q_j * Φ(r_ij) where Φ(r) = 1/r. In MPNNs, message sums M_i = Σ_j h_j * Φ(r_ij) where Φ is learned radial filters and h_j are atom embeddings. Ewald message passing exploits this analogy by decomposing the interaction kernel Φ into short-range Φ^sr (distance-truncated) and long-range Φ^lr (frequency-truncated) components. The key innovation is computing the long-range part in Fourier space: M^lr(x_i) = Σ_k exp(ik^T x_i) * s_k * Φ^lr(k), where s_k = Σ_j h_j exp(-ik^T x_j) are structure factor embeddings. This enables O(N_at * N_k) complexity with controllable N_k. For periodic systems (OC20), the method uses the reciprocal lattice from periodic boundary conditions, fixing the number of frequencies in each reciprocal basis direction rather than using a spherical cutoff. For aperiodic systems (OE62), it discretizes the Fourier domain using a voxel grid with resolution Δ=0.2 Å^-1. The method integrates with existing GNNs by adding long-range message passing as another contribution in the update equation: h_i^(l+1) = (1/√3)[h_i^(l) + f^sr(M_i^sr) + f^lr(M_i^lr)]. The frequency filters are learned via radial basis functions (aperiodic) or direct lattice-indexed weights (periodic). Tested on SchNet, PaiNN, DimeNet++, and GemNet-T with minimal architectural modifications.
content.experiment: The method was evaluated on two datasets: OC20 (265M periodic structures of adsorbate-catalyst combinations under 3D periodic boundary conditions, trained on OC20-2M subsplit) and OE62 (62K large organic molecules with DFT-D3 dispersion-corrected energies). Four baseline GNNs were tested: SchNet, PaiNN, DimeNet++, and GemNet-T. The evaluation included: (1) Energy MAE improvements with Ewald MP vs baselines; (2) Runtime overhead analysis; (3) Comparison against alternative strategies: increased distance cutoff, SchNet block with increased cutoff (replacing Ewald block), and increased embedding size (matching parameter count). On OC20, Ewald MP achieved average 10.3% energy MAE improvement across all models and test splits. On OE62, average improvement was 16.1%. The runtime overhead was comparable to or smaller than baseline model differences. Ewald MP consistently outperformed the large cutoff setting on OC20 and showed robust improvements where other strategies (large cutoff, SchNet LR block) had mixed or detrimental effects. A critical analysis on OE62 leveraged the fact that energy targets contain DFT-D3 dispersion correction: binning molecules by DFT-D3 value showed Ewald MP has outsize improvement for structures with high long-range contributions, and Ewald MP recovers or surpasses a 'cheating' baseline that explicitly adds DFT-D3 to predictions. Force MAE improvements on OC20 were consistent but small, explained by frequency truncation removing fast-changing high-frequency contributions that affect gradients.
content.result: Ewald message passing provides robust energy MAE improvements (10% on OC20, 16% on OE62) across all tested GNN architectures with acceptable runtime overhead. The method achieves better cost-performance tradeoff than simply increasing distance cutoffs or adding more parameters. Key finding: Ewald MP specifically targets long-range interactions, as evidenced by outsize improvements on structures with high DFT-D3 dispersion corrections and ability to match/surpass a baseline with explicit DFT-D3. The method is more efficient on periodic structures (OC20) where the reciprocal lattice provides natural discretization. For aperiodic systems, voxel discretization is required but maintains effectiveness. The approach is architecture-agnostic and can be integrated as a plug-and-play addition. Limitations: (1) Force prediction improvements are smaller due to frequency truncation removing high-frequency components; (2) The method introduces new hyperparameters (frequency cutoff, voxel resolution for aperiodic case); (3) For aperiodic systems, there may be a 'gap' of medium-range interactions not covered by either component. Future directions include adapting more efficient Ewald variants (FFT-based) for sub-quadratic scaling and exploring invariant filtering schemes for datasets with large supercell size variations.
content.dataset: OC20 (Open Catalyst 2020), OE62 (organic molecules with DFT-D3 corrections)
content.topic_relation: Directly relevant to Long_Short_Range_Message_Passing hypothesis (Rank 2) which posits that polymer physics is governed by multi-scale interplay of local covalent chemistry and global chain entanglement. This paper provides concrete evidence that explicit long-range modules yield 10-16% improvements. The method is physics-grounded (Ewald summation from computational chemistry) and architecture-agnostic, making it a strong candidate for polymer property prediction. The decomposition into short-range (distance-truncated) and long-range (frequency-truncated) mirrors the LSR-MP approach mentioned in the hypothesis space. The paper also touches on periodic systems (OC20) which relates to Graph_Transformer_for_Global_Topology hypothesis (Rank 1) about periodicity encoding.
content.topic_contribution: Provides validated evidence that explicit long-range message passing yields consistent 10-16% improvements across architectures. The Fourier-space approach with structure factor embeddings offers a concrete mechanism for capturing non-local interactions. For polymer Tg prediction, this could capture chain entanglement effects that extend beyond local covalent bonds. The method can be combined with periodicity-aware attention (Rank 1 hypothesis) since they address different aspects: periodicity encoding handles repeat unit symmetry, while Ewald MP handles long-range interactions. Actionable experiment: implement Ewald message passing on polymer Tg dataset, potentially combined with Matformer-style periodic invariance. The paper also validates that simple parameter scaling (increased embedding size) does not replicate the improvements, confirming the importance of architectural inductive bias over brute-force scaling.

memory.abstract: CELLI (Charge Equilibration Layer for Long-range Interactions) is a model-agnostic building block that generalizes the classical Qeq method to modern equivariant GNN MLIPs, enabling accurate modeling of long-range electrostatics and charge transfer while maintaining computational efficiency and interpretability through explicit charge predictions.
memory.keyword: long-range interactions, charge equilibration, equivariant GNN, MLIP, electrostatics

content.background: Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials (MLIPs) based on GNNs achieve near-quantum accuracy at linear computational cost, but suffer from inherent locality limitations. Strictly local MLIPs assume atomic interactions are dominated by immediate neighborhoods, while message-passing MLIPs propagate information beyond immediate environments but remain effectively local due to cutoff radii. This locality precludes modeling critical long-range effects: charge transfer, electrostatic interactions, and dispersion effects. These limitations are severe for real-world systems—protein folding involves interactions spanning up to 15Å, ionic liquids require accurate electrostatics, and molecular aggregation depends on long-range forces. Existing solutions have tradeoffs: reciprocal space methods (Fourier-based) struggle with differently oriented structures; Euclidean Fast Attention respects symmetries but requires expensive spherical integration; hierarchical message-passing methods (RANGE, Erwin) don't generalize to bulk systems; physics-driven approaches that add long-range corrections separately fail to capture the correlation between local environments and long-range effects. The CENT method addressed some challenges via Qeq with Behler-type neural networks, but requires hand-crafted descriptors and struggles with chemically diverse datasets.
content.method: CELLI introduces the classical Qeq method into equivariant GNN architectures through a novel architectural building block. The core innovation is splitting total energy U = U_Coul + ΔU, where U_Coul captures long-range electrostatics via charge equilibration and ΔU captures short-range corrections conditioned on charge environments. The architecture has four components: (1) Environment Embedding: MLPs predict per-edge contributions to electronegativity χ̃_ij and optionally hardness J̃_ij^R from scalar latent features x_ij^l. Summing over incident edges yields atom electronegativities χ_i = f·Σ_k χ̃_ik. (2) Species Embedding: Species-dependent hardness contributions J̃_i^Z are combined with environment-dependent contributions using generalized softplus σ_+(x_1,...,x_k) = log(1 + exp(x_1) + ... + exp(x_k)) to ensure positive hardnesses J_i. Charge radii are based on single-bond covalent radii with learned species-dependent scaling. (3) Qeq Method: Given electronegativities, hardnesses, and radii, Qeq solves a constrained quadratic optimization to minimize U_Qeq(R,Q) = U_Coul(R,Q) + Σ_i[χ_i·Q_i + J_ii/2·Q_i²] subject to charge conservation Σ_i Q_i = Q_tot. The solution involves solving a linear system with O(N³) complexity for small systems, or O(N log N) using SPME for periodic systems. (4) Charge Embedding: Equilibrated charges are embedded back into latent features via MLP_Q(Q_i, Q_j, c_i, c_j) and MLP_x to update scalar features x_ij^{l+1}, enabling subsequent layers to condition short-range interactions on the charge environment. CELLI is model-agnostic: for Allegro (strictly local), it's inserted between Interaction Layers; for MACE (message-passing), it processes scalar node features and provides weighted residual updates. The placement determines the body-order of environment descriptions passed to Qeq and the receptive field for charge-conditioned short-range learning.
content.experiment: The evaluation used four benchmark systems designed to be unsolvable by strictly local methods: (1) Carbon chains (C₁₀H₂ neutral and C₁₀H₃⁺ charged) testing long-range charge transfer from local perturbations; (2) Silver clusters (Ag₃ triangular and linear, +1 and -1 charges) testing charge-state-dependent geometry preferences; (3) NaCl clusters (Na₈Cl₈⁺ and Na₉Cl₈⁺) testing energy landscape accuracy along predefined paths; (4) Gold dimers on MgO(001) surfaces (undoped and Al-doped) testing adsorption energies in periodic charge-sensitive environments. All benchmarks used PBE functional DFT references with Hirshfeld charges. For generalization testing, the OE62 dataset (62,000 organic molecules, up to 174 atoms, 16 elements) evaluated scalability and chemical diversity. The SPICE dataset (peptides, drug-like molecules, 17 species) tested MD simulation stability over 1ns trajectories at 300K. Baselines included Allegro, MACE, 4G³, LRSR, CACE-LR, SpookyNet, DimeNet++ with Ewald/Neural P³M, and PaiNN with Ewald/Neural P³M. Models were trained via force matching with ADAM optimizer, polynomial learning rate schedule, and species-dependent energy shifts. Hyperparameters matched prior work for fair comparison.
content.result: CELLI achieves state-of-the-art results on all benchmark systems with strictly local models. On carbon chains: energy RMSE 0.599 meV/atom vs Allegro baseline 0.772, force RMSE 31.00 meV/Å vs 49.18. On silver clusters: energy RMSE 0.80 meV/atom vs baseline 199.25 (catastrophic failure), demonstrating CELLI captures charge-state dependence. On NaCl clusters: energy RMSE 0.127 meV/atom vs 1.612, correctly identifying distinct minima for different charge states. On gold dimers: energy RMSE 0.077 meV/atom vs 2.329. Environment-dependent hardness variant (CELLI-J^R) generally outperformed species-dependent hardness. For message-passing models, CELLI-MACE(6) achieves 0.128 meV/atom on carbon chains vs baseline 0.335, comparable to SpookyNet(6). On OE62, CELLI-Allegro-S achieves 55.3 meV MAE vs baseline 63.4 meV, comparable to DimeNet++ with Neural P³M (41.5 meV MAE) but with ~2× faster inference. CELLI adds only marginal computational overhead (determined by underlying architecture) and maintains stable 1ns MD simulations on SPICE without bond breakage or particle overlap. Key insight: partial charge prediction accuracy doesn't correlate strongly with energy/force accuracy, suggesting charge partitioning schemes may constrain expressiveness. The predicted electronegativities, hardnesses, and atomic radii correlate well with literature values, confirming physical interpretability.
content.dataset: Four benchmark systems (carbon chains, silver clusters, NaCl clusters, gold dimers on MgO) from Ko et al.; OE62 dataset (62,000 organic molecules); SPICE dataset v2.0.1 (peptides, drug-like molecules)
content.topic_relation: Directly addresses Long_Short_Range_Message_Passing hypothesis (Rank 2) which posits that polymer physics is governed by multi-scale interplay of local covalent chemistry and global chain entanglement. The paper validates that explicit long-range modules provide significant improvements (40% in LSR-MP, similar gains here). CELLI provides a physics-grounded, interpretable mechanism for capturing non-local interactions through charge equilibration. The gap decomposition analysis estimated ~1-2 RMSE of the 6.24 RMSE gap (FP-PGNN 37.04 vs PerioGT 30.8) may come from missing long-range interactions—CELLI offers a concrete approach to recover this. The method's model-agnostic nature allows integration with existing polymer GNN architectures.
content.topic_contribution: CELLI provides an actionable architecture for incorporating long-range interactions into polymer property prediction models. Key design choices transferable to polymers: (1) Qeq-based charge equilibration is physically interpretable and doesn't require hand-crafted descriptors; (2) Environment-dependent electronegativities and hardnesses learned from GNN features enable chemical diversity; (3) The charge embedding mechanism allows conditioning short-range predictions on global charge state. For polymer Tg prediction, CELLI could capture long-range entanglement effects through charge redistribution across repeat units. The marginal computational overhead (~2× faster than DimeNet++ with similar accuracy) is suitable for polymer-scale systems. Future experiment: integrate CELLI with periodic-invariant attention (from Matformer/PerioGT) to simultaneously address periodicity (dominant ~4-5 RMSE) and long-range interactions (~1-2 RMSE) in the gap decomposition.

memory.abstract: Matformer introduces periodic invariance and periodic pattern encoding for crystal material property prediction, achieving SOTA on Materials Project and JARVIS benchmarks through radius-based multi-edge graph construction satisfying periodic invariance, and self-connecting edges encoding lattice geometry.
memory.keyword: periodic invariance, crystal graph transformer, periodic pattern encoding, edge-wise attention, self-connecting edges

content.background: Crystal material property prediction faces unique challenges distinct from molecular graph learning. While molecules are finite structures, crystals consist of minimum unit cells repeating infinitely on regular lattices in 3D space, requiring periodic graph representations. Existing methods like CGCNN, SchNet, MEGNET, GATGNN, and ALIGNN either break periodic invariance or fail to explicitly encode periodic patterns. E(3) invariance (invariance to translation, rotation, reflection) is insufficient for crystals—periodic invariance requires representations to be invariant to both scaling of unit cells AND shifts of periodic boundaries. When boundaries shift, the same crystal can yield completely different graph structures if periodic invariance is violated. Furthermore, lattice matrices L = [ℓ₁, ℓ₂, ℓ₃]ᵀ encoding periodic repeating patterns are critical—different lattice sizes and orientations correspond to different materials even with identical unit cell structures. Prior multi-edge graph construction captures local interactions but ignores these periodic patterns entirely. Graphormer, successful on molecular tasks, breaks periodic invariance by treating atoms as single nodes, causing 53% MAE degradation on crystal tasks.
content.method: Matformer addresses both periodic invariance and periodic pattern encoding through two key innovations. First, for periodic invariant graph construction, the paper proposes two methods: (1) Radius-based multi-edge graph construction—each node i represents atom i and ALL its periodic duplicates at positions {pᵢ + k₁ℓ₁ + k₂ℓ₂ + k₃ℓ₃ | k₁,k₂,k₃∈ℤ}. Edges are built from node j to i for ALL positions of j within radius r of i, using Euclidean distance dⱼᵢ = ||pⱼ + k'₁ℓ₁ + k'₂ℓ₂ + k'₃ℓ₃ - pᵢ||₂ ≤ r. This guarantees periodic invariance because all pairwise distances are invariant to boundary shifts. (2) Fully-connected construction—connects every pair with t smallest distances across all periodic images. The paper proves both methods satisfy periodic invariance mathematically. Second, for periodic pattern encoding, Matformer adds 6 self-connecting edges per atom encoding lattice geometry: ||ℓ₁||₂, ||ℓ₂||₂, ||ℓ₃||₂, ||ℓ₁+ℓ₂||₂, ||ℓ₂+ℓ₃||₂, ||ℓ₁+ℓ₃||₂. These six distances completely determine the lattice shape—three edge lengths and three angles between lattice vectors. The message passing uses edge-wise attention: qᵢⱼʰ = (qᵢ|qᵢ|qᵢ), kᵢⱼʰ = (kᵢ|kⱼ|eᵢⱼʰ'), αᵢⱼʰ = (qᵢⱼʰ ∘ kᵢⱼʰ)/√d, where query attends to key, neighbor key, and edge features simultaneously. Critically, softmax is REPLACED by sigmoid + layer normalization to preserve node degree information in multi-edge graphs. The final message mᵢⱼʰ = sigmoid(LNorm(αᵢⱼʰ)) ∘ LN_update(vᵢ|vⱼ|eᵢⱼʰ'). This edge-wise attention differs from Graphormer's node-wise attention and handles multi-edge graphs naturally.
content.experiment: Experiments conducted on two major benchmarks: Materials Project (69,239 crystals for formation energy/band gap; 4,664 crystals for bulk/shear moduli) and JARVIS (44,578 crystals for formation energy/total energy/bandgap(OPT); 14,537 for bandgap(MBJ); 44,296 for Ehull). Baselines include CFID, CGCNN, SchNet, MEGNET, GATGNN, and ALIGNN. All models retrained with identical train/val/test splits for fair comparison. Matformer uses 5 layers, 4 attention heads, 128-dim embeddings, 12 nearest neighbors for radius computation, Adam optimizer with weight decay 1e-5, one-cycle learning rate scheduler, batch size 64. Ablation studies on JARVIS formation energy: (1) Periodic invariance: OCgraph (Graphormer's construction, breaks periodic invariance) gives MAE 0.0530 vs radius multi-edge (periodic invariant) 0.0348—a 53% degradation from breaking periodic invariance. (2) Periodic encoding: removing self-connecting edges degrades MAE from 0.0325 to 0.0337, demonstrating explicit pattern encoding matters. (3) Graph construction: radius-based (0.0325) outperforms t-fully-connected (0.0402). (4) Attention mechanism: sigmoid+layernorm (0.0325) outperforms softmax-scalar (0.0376) and softmax-vector (0.0347), validating that preserving degree information is critical. (5) Angular information: adding angle encoding increases training time 3× without performance gain, suggesting periodic patterns already capture sufficient structural information.
content.result: Matformer achieves SOTA on all tasks: Materials Project formation energy (0.021 vs ALIGNN 0.022 eV/atom), band gap (0.211 vs 0.218 eV), bulk moduli (0.043 vs 0.051 log(GPa)), shear moduli (0.073 vs 0.078 log(GPa)); JARVIS formation energy (0.0325 vs 0.0331 eV/atom), bandgap(OPT) (0.137 vs 0.142 eV), total energy (0.035 vs 0.037 eV/atom), Ehull (0.064 vs 0.076 eV, 15.8% improvement), bandgap(MBJ) (0.30 vs 0.31 eV). Efficiency: 3× faster training (8.9h vs 27.3h) and inference (59s vs 156s) than ALIGNN with smaller model size (11.0 MB vs 15.4 MB). Energy within Threshold (EwT) metric shows Matformer excels at high-precision predictions—EwT(0.01) improves 5.92% on Materials Project formation energy. Key principles validated: (1) Periodic invariance is FUNDAMENTAL—breaking it causes 53% degradation; (2) Periodicity encoding belongs in attention mechanism design (periodic invariance in attention weights via edge-wise attention), NOT in graph topology modifications; (3) Self-connecting edges encoding lattice geometry are more effective than angular information for crystal representation; (4) Multi-edge graphs require edge-wise attention without softmax to preserve degree information. Limitations: angular information integration remains challenging for periodic graphs; negative societal impacts of material discovery apply.

memory.content:
## Day 3 Experiment: PIPGA - Negative Result

### Hypothesis
Matformer-style periodic invariance (edge-wise attention without softmax, multi-edge graphs, self-connecting edges) would recover ~4-5 RMSE gap to SOTA for polymer Tg prediction.

### Implementation
- **Multi-edge graph**: 3-copy extension (left/center/right), k-hop neighbors with periodic offset k ∈ {-1, 0, +1}
- **Edge-wise attention**: sigmoid((q ∘ k) / √d) + LayerNorm, NO softmax
- **Self-connecting edges**: d_head, d_tail distance encoding for periodic geometry
- **ECFP4 modulation**: Fingerprint gates attention weights

### Results (5-fold CV)

| Model | Test RMSE | Ablation Impact |
|-------|-----------|-----------------|
| Full PIPGA | 38.99 ± 2.10 | Baseline |
| No Fingerprint | 64.71 ± 4.45 | +25.72 (CRITICAL) |
| Softmax Attention | 41.47 ± 3.51 | +2.48 |
| No Self-Loop | 39.93 ± 1.79 | +0.95 |
| Single Edge | 39.09 ± 2.14 | +0.11 |

**Target: < 34.0 RMSE | Achieved: 38.99 | FAILED by 4.99 points**

### Critical Findings

1. **Fingerprint Dominance**: ECFP4 provides +25.72 RMSE contribution (66% of model performance). The GNN is essentially a weak enhancement to fingerprint-based prediction.

2. **Periodic Invariance FAILED**: 
   - Multi-edge mechanism: +0.11 RMSE (negligible, within noise)
   - Self-connecting edges: +0.95 RMSE (minor benefit)
   - **The core Matformer adaptation did NOT work for 1D polymers**

3. **Edge-wise Attention Works**: Sigmoid attention (+2.48 RMSE over softmax) validates the multi-edge handling design, but this is not the dominant factor.

4. **Training Instability**: Best epochs range from 1-86 across folds, indicating convergence issues.

### Why It Failed

1. **Fundamental Mismatch**: Matformer's periodic invariance is designed for 3D crystal lattices with translational symmetry in all directions. 1D polymer chains have fundamentally different periodicity (linear chain with head/tail connectivity vs. 3D unit cell).

2. **Multi-edge Redundancy**: In 1D polymers, atoms near boundaries already have explicit connections to head/tail atoms. The 3-copy extension creates redundant edges that don't add new information.

3. **Distance Encoding Insufficient**: Self-connecting edges with d_head/d_tail provide positional information, but this is already captured by standard atom features in a linear chain.

4. **Over-Engineering**: The complex periodic invariance mechanisms (+0.11 RMSE) are over-engineered for a problem where simple fingerprints (+25.72 RMSE) dominate.

### Implications for Hypothesis Space

**Graph_Transformer_for_Global_Topology [NEEDS REVISION]**:
- Matformer-style periodic invariance does NOT transfer from 3D crystals to 1D polymers
- Periodicity encoding in attention mechanism is NOT the key to polymer Tg prediction
- PerioGT's SOTA performance (30.8 RMSE) must come from other mechanisms, not just periodicity

**Gap Decomposition Update**:
- Original estimate: ~4-5 RMSE from periodicity encoding
- Actual finding: ~0.1-1.0 RMSE from periodicity mechanisms
- **The 6.24 RMSE gap (37.04 → 30.8) remains unexplained**

### Lessons Learned

1. **Negative Results Are Valuable**: Clear demonstration that Matformer adaptation fails for 1D polymers saves future exploration time.

2. **Ablation Studies Critical**: Without ablations, we might have attributed the 38.99 RMSE to "partial success" rather than recognizing fingerprint dominance.

3. **Domain Transfer Requires Validation**: Mechanisms from 3D crystal graphs don't automatically transfer to 1D polymer chains.

4. **Simple Baselines Are Strong**: ECFP4 + LightGBM (38.78 RMSE) is competitive with complex GNN (38.99 RMSE).

### Next Steps

1. **Investigate PerioGT Architecture**: Read PerioGT paper carefully to understand what actually works (not just "periodicity-aware attention").

2. **Long-Range Interactions**: Focus on LSR-MP-style long-range message passing instead of periodicity encoding.

3. **Fingerprint-First Approach**: Accept fingerprint dominance and design lightweight GNN to complement, not replace, fingerprint features.

4. **Alternative Periodicity**: Consider frequency-domain representations or learned periodic embeddings instead of graph construction.

daily_journal.journal:
## Day 1 Journal: 2026-03-19

### Literature Review
Selected and analyzed 4 papers: PolyConf (hierarchical polymer conformation generation), Open Polymer Challenge (distribution shifts in polymer prediction), LSR-MP (long-short range message passing for non-local interactions), and PerioGT (periodicity-aware graph transformer achieving SOTA on Tg/Tm/Egc). Key insight: fingerprint+tree models dominated the competition, and PerioGT's periodicity-aware attention achieves current SOTA.

### Hypothesis Test: Data_Centric_Foundation
**REJECTED with high confidence.** Executed the foundational hypothesis that data quality issues explain the baseline-to-SOTA gap. Results showed the Tg dataset is remarkably clean: 100% valid SMILES, zero duplicates, no statistical outliers. The 26% performance gap (MLP+ECFP4 at 38.78 RMSE vs PerioGT SOTA at 30.8) is due to algorithmic sophistication, not data artifacts.

### Baselines Established
- MLP with ECFP4 fingerprints: RMSE 38.78°C (R²=0.8781) — beats reported GAT baseline (50.5)
- Simple GCN: RMSE 45.69°C (R²=0.8307)
- Key finding: Fingerprint features encode substructure information that simple graph message passing misses

### Multimer Generation Attempt
Failed with 6-13% success rate using naive SMILES concatenation. Requires sophisticated polymer chain assembly algorithms (PolyConf-style hierarchical approach).

### Hypothesis Updates
- Data_Centric_Foundation: REJECTED
- Graph_Transformer_for_Global_Topology: Elevated to Rank 1 (validated by PerioGT SOTA)
- Long_Short_Range_Message_Passing: Elevated to Rank 2 (validated by LSR-MP 40% improvement)
- Self_Supervised_3D_Multimer_Pretraining: Rank 3, conditional on solving multimer assembly
- DMPNN_for_Local_Valency: Deprioritized to Rank 4

### Ideas Generated for Day 2
Reasonable: (1) Fingerprint-Periodic Graph Fusion via attention, (2) Hierarchical Atom-RepeatUnit Message Passing adapted from LSR-MP. Concept-leaping: (1) Cyclic Contrastive Learning exploiting polymer repeat unit symmetry, (2) Polymer Band Structure using graph Laplacian eigenvalues as 1D crystal representation.

## Day 2 Journal: 2026-03-20

### Literature Review
Selected 4 papers aligned with Rank 1 hypothesis (Graph Transformer for Global Topology): Matformer (periodic invariance for crystals, 53% MAE degradation when broken), MoCL (domain knowledge augmentations for contrastive learning), GPIP (geometry-enhanced pretraining, 10× data efficiency), and SIMG (stereoelectronics-infused graphs with small-molecule-to-protein extrapolation). Key insight: Matformer provides theoretical foundation—periodicity encoding must be in attention mechanism design (periodic invariance), not graph topology modifications.

### Experiment: FP-PGNN (Fingerprint-Periodic Graph Neural Network)
Executed the Day 1 idea of fusing ECFP4 fingerprints with periodic graph attention. Results:

| Model | RMSE | Finding |
|-------|------|---------|
| Full FP-PGNN | **37.04 ± 0.68** | Beats baseline |
| No fingerprint | 42.67 ± 2.06 | Fingerprint: **+5.64 RMSE** |
| No periodic edges | 37.33 ± 0.73 | Periodic: **+0.29 RMSE** |

**Validated:** Fingerprint contribution is dominant (+5.64 RMSE, 19× larger than periodic edges), explaining why MLP+ECFP4 (38.78) vastly outperforms GCN (45.69).

**Failed:** Simple virtual edges between head/tail atoms contribute minimally (+0.29 RMSE). Periodicity encoding belongs in attention weights (Matformer-style periodic invariance), not graph topology.

### Hypothesis Updates
- Graph_Transformer_for_Global_Topology: **REFINED** — periodicity in attention mechanism, not topology
- Long_Short_Range_Message_Passing: **ELEVATED** — ~1-2 RMSE of gap may come from long-range interactions
- Gap decomposition: ~4-5 RMSE from periodicity, ~1-2 from long-range

### Ideas Generated for Day 3
**Reasonable:** (1) PIPGA — Periodic-Invariant Polymer Graph Attention with Matformer-style edge-wise attention, (2) FMPA — Fingerprint-Modulated Periodic Attention. **Concept-leaping:** (1) TBSE — Tight-Binding Spectral Encoder (chemistry-aware Hamiltonian replaces chemically-blind Laplacian), (2) TIDE — Transfer Integral Distribution Encoder (physics-grounded chain rigidity → Tg).

### Progress
Current: 37.04 RMSE → SOTA: 30.8 RMSE (gap: 6.24). Estimated ~4-5 RMSE recoverable from proper periodicity encoding in attention.

## Day 3 Journal: 2026-03-21

### Literature Review
Deep dive into Matformer paper to understand periodic invariance mechanism for adaptation to 1D polymers.

### Experiment: PIPGA (Periodic-Invariant Polymer Graph Attention)
Executed comprehensive Matformer-style adaptation with 5-fold CV and 5 ablations. Results:

| Model | Test RMSE | Ablation Impact |
|-------|-----------|-----------------|
| Full PIPGA | **38.99 ± 2.10** | Baseline |
| No Fingerprint | 64.71 ± 4.45 | +25.72 (CRITICAL) |
| Softmax Attention | 41.47 ± 3.51 | +2.48 |
| No Self-Loop | 39.93 ± 1.79 | +0.95 |
| Single Edge | 39.09 ± 2.14 | +0.11 |

**Target: < 34.0 RMSE | Achieved: 38.99 | FAILED by 4.99 points**

### Critical Negative Result

**Matformer-style periodic invariance does NOT work for 1D polymers:**
- Multi-edge mechanism: +0.11 RMSE (negligible, within noise)
- Self-connecting edges: +0.95 RMSE (minor benefit)
- The core adaptation FAILED to transfer from 3D crystals to 1D polymer chains

### Root Cause Analysis

1. **Fundamental Mismatch**: Matformer designed for 3D crystal lattices with translational symmetry in all directions. 1D polymer chains have fundamentally different periodicity (linear chain with head/tail vs 3D unit cell).

2. **Multi-edge Redundancy**: In 1D polymers, atoms near boundaries already have explicit connections to head/tail atoms. The 3-copy extension creates redundant edges that do not add new information.

3. **Fingerprint Dominance**: ECFP4 provides +25.72 RMSE (66% of performance). The GNN is a weak enhancement to fingerprint-based prediction.

### Hypothesis Updates
- Graph_Transformer_for_Global_Topology: **NEEDS REVISION** — Matformer periodicity does NOT transfer to 1D polymers. PerioGT SOTA mechanism remains unexplained.
- Long_Short_Range_Message_Passing: **ELEVATED to RANK 1** — Periodicity failed, long-range interactions may be key.
- Gap decomposition revised: ~0.1-1.0 RMSE from periodicity (NOT 4-5), ~1-2 RMSE from long-range, ~4-5 RMSE from unknown mechanism.

### Ideas Generated for Day 4
**Reasonable:** (1) Investigate PerioGT architecture in detail, (2) LSR-MP long-range message passing for polymer entanglement. **Concept-leaping:** (1) Transformer with global attention (no periodicity assumption), (2) Contrastive learning with polymer-specific augmentations.

### Progress
Current: 38.99 RMSE (PIPGA) → SOTA: 30.8 RMSE (gap: 8.19). Matformer adaptation failed. Need to investigate what actually makes PerioGT work.

content.hypothesis_elevation_rationale: With periodicity encoding failed (mem_102), long-range interactions become the leading hypothesis for the unexplained 8.19 RMSE gap. The evidence from Ewald MP (10-16% improvement), CELLI (SOTA on long-range benchmarks), and LSR-MP (40% improvement) provides multiple validated architectural approaches. The polymer physics rationale (entanglement, cooperative motion) strongly supports this hypothesis.
content.narrative: The Day 3 literature review (mem_098, mem_099, mem_100) combined with the PIPGA negative result (mem_102) elevates Long_Short_Range_Message_Passing to Rank 1. Three independent papers demonstrate that explicit long-range mechanisms yield substantial improvements: Ewald MP uses Fourier-space frequency cutoffs for 10-16% energy MAE improvement (mem_099); CELLI enables accurate long-range electrostatics through charge equilibration (mem_100); PointGAT shows 3D geometry adds meaningful signal beyond graph attention (mem_098). Combined with LSR-MP's 40% improvement through bipartite atom-fragment message passing (mem_075), the evidence is compelling. For polymer Tg prediction, long-range interactions are physically motivated: entanglement involves chain segments 10-100+ atoms apart, and glass transition depends on cooperative segment motion requiring long-range coordination. ECFP4 fingerprints (+25.72 RMSE) capture local substructures but not global chain topology. The 8.19 RMSE gap may represent missing entanglement effects. The actionable architecture is clear: implement LSR-MP style bipartite message passing with repeat units as fragment nodes, potentially combined with Ewald-style Fourier-space long-range or CELLI-style charge equilibration. This hypothesis has stronger evidential support than the failed periodicity encoding hypothesis.

memory.abstract: Fingerprint Dominance Confirmed: ECFP4 provides +25.72 RMSE (66% of model performance) in PIPGA experiment. The GNN component contributes minimally. This forces a strategic pivot: design lightweight GNN to complement fingerprints, not replace them. content.consensus: The PIPGA ablation (mem_102) definitively confirms fingerprint dominance: ECFP4 contributes +25.72 RMSE (66% of model performance), while the entire GNN architecture (multi-edge, self-loop, edge-wise attention) contributes only ~2-3 RMSE combined. The pattern is consistent: fingerprints capture the dominant signal, GNN provides marginal enhancement.

memory.abstract: Long-Range Entanglement-Aware Message Passing (LEMP): Bipartite atom-repeat-unit architecture adapted from LSR-MP to capture polymer chain entanglement effects that ECFP4 fingerprints miss.
memory.keyword: long-range interactions, polymer entanglement, bipartite message passing, LSR-MP adaptation

H: H1: Polymer Tg depends on chain mobility which is governed by entanglement effects between chain segments 10-100+ atoms apart - beyond the local substructures captured by ECFP4 fingerprints.
H2: Standard GNNs with fixed cutoff radius suffer from over-squashing when information from distant atoms must traverse many hops, missing the long-range correlations critical for entanglement.

H3: Bipartite message passing between atoms and repeat-unit nodes creates shortcut paths that alleviate over-squashing while encoding polymer-specific hierarchical structure (atoms → repeat units → chain).
H4: The ~1-3 RMSE gap component attributed to long-range interactions can be recovered through explicit long-range modules, independent of periodicity encoding.
content.X:
Implement Long-Range Entanglement-Aware Message Passing (LEMP) with fingerprint integration:

**Architecture Design:**
1. **Short-Range Module (Local Chemistry)**: 2-layer GIN on atom-level graph with 5-hop cutoff, encoding local covalent chemistry already partially captured by ECFP4.

2. **Repeat-Unit Fragmentation**: Each repeat unit forms a single fragment node. Fragment embedding H_RU = Mean(h_atoms_in_RU) + positional encoding for chain order. This is polymer-specific adaptation of LSR-MP's BRICS fragmentation.

3. **Long-Range Module (Entanglement)**: Bipartite graph connecting ALL atoms to ALL repeat-unit nodes (no cutoff). Each atom receives global context from all parts of the polymer chain. Message: m_i = Σ_j A_ij · W · H_RU_j where A_ij is distance-dependent attention (atoms attend to RUs based on graph distance).

4. **Fingerprint Integration**: ECFP4 (2048 bits) → MLP → h_fp. Concatenate [h_short, h_long, h_fp] for final prediction. This preserves fingerprint dominance while adding long-range signal.

5. **Training**: 5-fold CV on Tg dataset. Compare: (a) Full LEMP, (b) No long-range module, (c) No fingerprint, (d) Different RU fragmentation strategies.

**Target**: Recover ~1-3 RMSE from long-range interactions. If successful, LEMP should achieve ~35-37 RMSE (current PIPGA 38.99 minus long-range contribution).

**Compute**: ~0.8M parameters, trainable on single 2080Ti in <3 hours.
Y: Y1: If H3 is correct, LEMP with long-range module will outperform LEMP without long-range by >1.5 RMSE, confirming that explicit entanglement capture improves Tg prediction.

Y2: If H4 is correct, the improvement from long-range module will be additive to fingerprint contribution (+25.72 RMSE), not replacing it. Ablation: remove fingerprint should still show +20+ RMSE degradation.
Y3: Attention visualization should show atoms attending to distant repeat units (not just local neighborhood), providing evidence that long-range dependencies are captured.
Y4: Compare LEMP against PerioGT SOTA (30.8). If LEMP achieves ~35-37 RMSE, this validates long-range hypothesis and leaves ~5 RMSE gap for other mechanisms (likely PA-based contrastive learning).

Y5: If LEMP fails to improve over PIPGA (38.99), this suggests the Tg dataset (7170 samples) is too small for long-range architectures to show advantage, and pre-training approaches (like PerioGT's PA contrastive) may be necessary.

memory.abstract: Periodicity-Augmented Fine-tuning (PAFT): Adapt PerioGT's critical PA-based contrastive learning mechanism for supervised fine-tuning without requiring PI1M pre-training, targeting the ~5-7 RMSE unknown mechanism gap.
memory.keyword: periodicity augmentation, contrastive learning, fine-tuning, PerioGT mechanism, data augmentation

H: H1: PerioGT's SOTA performance (30.8 RMSE) comes primarily from Periodicity Augmentation (PA)-based contrastive learning, NOT from periodicity-aware attention mechanisms - the ablation shows PA is the most critical component.

H2: PA generates multiple valid repeat unit views through sliding window sampling along the polymer backbone, creating chemically equivalent representations that the model learns to map to similar embeddings.
H3: The PA mechanism can be adapted for supervised fine-tuning without requiring large-scale self-supervised pre-training on PI1M, by using PA as data augmentation during supervised training.

H4: The ~5-7 RMSE gap (unknown mechanism) is primarily due to missing periodicity-aware representations that contrastive learning provides - this is orthogonal to long-range interactions and fingerprint contributions.
content.X:
Implement Periodicity-Augmented Fine-tuning (PAFT) combining supervised learning with PA-based contrastive regularization:

**PA Mechanism (from PerioGT):**
For each polymer repeat unit SMILES, generate K augmented views by:
1. Parse p-SMILES to identify backbone atoms
2. Slide a sampling box (size = backbone atoms / 2) along the backbone
3. Generate valid RU fragments representing the same polymer
4. These are chemically equivalent representations with different 'cut points'

**Training Objective:**
L_total = L_supervised + λ * L_contrastive

Where:
- L_supervised = MSE(predicted_Tg, actual_Tg) for original RU
- L_contrastive = InfoNCE loss pulling augmented views together, pushing different polymers apart
- λ balances supervised and contrastive objectives

**Architecture:**
- Backbone: Simple GNN (2-layer GIN or GAT) - avoid over-engineering
- Fingerprint: ECFP4 (2048 bits) concatenated with graph embedding
- Projection head: 2-layer MLP for contrastive learning
- Prediction head: 2-layer MLP for Tg regression

**Implementation Details:**
1. Generate K=2 augmented views per polymer during training
2. Use 50% random masking (as in PerioGT) to prevent over-reliance on obvious differences
3. Contrastive temperature τ=0.1
4. Balance factor λ=0.5 (tune on validation set)
5. Train with 5-fold CV on Tg dataset

**Ablation Conditions:**
(a) Full PAFT with contrastive loss
(b) PA as data augmentation only (no contrastive loss, just average predictions)
(c) No PA (baseline)
(d) Different K values (1, 2, 4 augmented views)

**Target**: Recover ~3-5 RMSE from periodicity-aware representations. If successful, PAFT should achieve ~33-35 RMSE.
Y: Y1: If H1 and H3 are correct, PAFT with contrastive loss will outperform baseline (no PA) by >2 RMSE, confirming that PA mechanism is transferable to supervised fine-tuning.
Y2: If H2 is correct, augmented views from PA should have high Tanimoto similarity (>0.8) and similar predicted Tg values, demonstrating the model learns periodicity-aware representations.

Y3: Ablation comparing PA with contrastive loss vs PA as simple augmentation (averaging predictions) will show contrastive loss provides additional benefit, validating the representation learning aspect.
Y4: Compare PAFT against PerioGT SOTA (30.8). If PAFT achieves ~33-35 RMSE without PI1M pre-training, this validates that PA mechanism is the key, not the scale of pre-training.
Y5: If PAFT fails to improve over baseline, this suggests PerioGT's SOTA requires the full self-supervised pre-training pipeline (PA + masked node modeling + PI1M scale), not just PA augmentation.

memory.abstract: Spectral Chain Topology Encoding: Predicting Tg through Fourier-transformed chain sequences and Laplacian eigenvalue spectra - a representation-level intervention that encodes periodicity by mathematical construction rather than learned attention.
memory.keyword: spectral representation, Fourier features, Laplacian eigenvalues, chain topology, periodicity by construction

H: H1: The 8.19 RMSE gap is a REPRESENTATION problem, not an architecture problem. ECFP4 fingerprints encode local substructures (radius-2 circular neighborhoods) but completely miss CHAIN-LEVEL topology. No amount of architectural sophistication can recover information that doesn't exist in the input representation.

H2: Polymer periodicity is naturally encoded in spectral domain (Fourier coefficients of chain sequence, Laplacian eigenvalues of repeat unit graph). Solid-state physics has used k-space representations for 80+ years because periodicity is automatic in reciprocal space - no learning required.

H3: The spectral representation provides information ORTHOGONAL to ECFP4: (a) Fourier coefficients encode global chain periodicity and sequence patterns; (b) Laplacian eigenvalue spectrum encodes connectivity and flexibility modes; (c) Spectral gap (λ₂-λ₁) directly measures backbone rigidity.

H4: PerioGT's unexplained SOTA performance may come from implicit spectral information - the periodic graph construction creates a structure whose Laplacian has different eigenvalue spectrum than standard molecular graphs. The 'periodicity-aware attention' explanation is incomplete.
content.X:
Implement Spectral Chain Topology Encoder (SCTE) with three complementary spectral representations:

**Component 1: Fourier Chain Sequence Encoding**
- Parse repeat unit to extract backbone atom sequence (main chain atoms excluding side groups)
- Encode each backbone atom as feature vector: atom type (C, O, N, etc.), hybridization, bond types to neighbors
- Apply 1D FFT to the sequence: F(k) = Σ f(n) exp(-2πikn/N)
- Extract: (a) Low-frequency coefficients (k=1,2,3) capturing global chain patterns; (b) Power spectrum |F(k)|²; (c) Phase information
- Rationale: Fourier basis is PERIODIC BY CONSTRUCTION - no need to learn periodicity

**Component 2: Laplacian Eigenvalue Spectrum**
- Compute normalized graph Laplacian L = D^(-1/2)(D-A)D^(-1/2) for repeat unit
- Extract eigenvalues λ₁ ≤ λ₂ ≤ ... ≤ λₖ (k=20)
- Compute spectral features: (a) Spectral gap λ₂-λ₁ (rigidity measure); (b) Spectral radius λₘₐₓ; (c) Eigenvalue distribution moments; (d) Fiedler vector (λ₂ eigenvector) statistics
- Rationale: Eigenvalue spectrum encodes global connectivity independent of local features

**Component 3: Periodic Graph Spectrum**
- Construct periodic graph (add edge between head/tail atoms as in mem_052)
- Compute Laplacian eigenvalues of periodic graph
- Compare with non-periodic graph spectrum: the DIFFERENCE encodes periodicity-specific information
- Rationale: Directly measures how periodicity changes the spectral representation

**Architecture:**
- SCTE features (50-100 dims) + ECFP4 (2048 dims) → LightGBM
- Alternative: SCTE → MLP (2 layers, 64 hidden) → concatenate with ECFP4 → MLP
- Total parameters: <0.3M

**Training:** 5-fold CV on Tg dataset. Compare: (a) SCTE alone, (b) SCTE + ECFP4, (c) ECFP4 baseline (38.78), (d) PIPGA (38.99). Target: SCTE + ECFP4 < 33.0 RMSE.

**Ablation Conditions:**
- Fourier features only (no Laplacian)
- Laplacian features only (no Fourier)
- Periodic graph spectrum only
- All three combined
- Random spectral features (control)
Y: Y1: If H1 correct, SCTE + ECFP4 will outperform ECFP4 alone by >3 RMSE, demonstrating that chain-level spectral information fills the representation gap that architectural innovations failed to address.

Y2: If H2 correct, Fourier coefficients will show strong correlation with Tg for periodic polymers (backbone sequences with repeating patterns), while Laplacian eigenvalues will correlate with Tg for all polymers (rigidity measure).
Y3: If H3 correct, spectral gap (λ₂-λ₁) will show strong negative correlation with Tg (larger gap = more rigid = higher Tg), providing interpretable physics connection.

Y4: If H4 correct, the periodic graph spectrum will capture information that explains part of PerioGT's success - the difference between periodic and non-periodic Laplacian spectra will correlate with the 8.19 RMSE gap.

Y5: Feature importance analysis should reveal: (a) Low-frequency Fourier coefficients are most predictive (global chain patterns); (b) Spectral gap is among top features (rigidity); (c) These features are orthogonal to ECFP4 substructure features.

Y6: If SCTE fails to improve over ECFP4, this would suggest the 8.19 RMSE gap is NOT about representation - it would force reconsideration of what PerioGT actually does (potentially pre-training effects, data augmentation, or other mechanisms).

Y7: Success would establish a paradigm shift: instead of designing ever-more-complex architectures to learn periodicity, use representations where periodicity is encoded by mathematical construction - a principle that should have been obvious from 80+ years of solid-state physics.

memory.abstract: Conformational Rigidity Intermediate Prediction: Reframing Tg prediction as a two-stage problem - first predict chain rigidity (rotatable bonds, steric hindrance, conjugation) from structure, then map rigidity to Tg - providing interpretability and potentially closing the performance gap.
memory.keyword: intermediate property, chain rigidity, conformational entropy, interpretable prediction, two-stage model

H: H1: Tg is NOT directly predictable from molecular structure - it is determined by chain mobility/rigidity, which IS directly predictable. Current approaches try to learn the complex structure→Tg mapping in one step, missing the physics intermediate.

H2: Chain rigidity can be quantified by computable intermediate properties: (a) Rotatable bond fraction (f_rot = N_rotatable / N_total_bonds); (b) Steric hindrance index (volume of side groups near backbone); (c) Conjugation extent (π-electron delocalization length); (d) Persistence length proxy (from 2D structure estimation).

H3: The structure→rigidity mapping is LEARNABLE with simple models (linear or shallow networks) because it depends on local geometry. The rigidity→Tg mapping follows polymer physics (Flory-Fox equation, WLF equation) and can be modeled analytically or with simple regression.

H4: PerioGT's unexplained success may come from implicitly learning rigidity features through its contrastive pre-training - augmented views with different periodicity samplings may force the model to learn rigidity-invariant representations.

H5: ECFP4 fingerprints partially capture rigidity information (aromatic rings, functional groups) but miss the GLOBAL integration of local flexibility/rigidity into chain-level properties. This explains why ECFP4 provides 66% of performance but can't close the gap.
content.X:
Implement Conformational Rigidity Intermediate Predictor (CRIP) as a two-stage model:

**Stage 1: Rigidity Feature Extraction**
Compute physics-based rigidity features from repeat unit structure:

1. **Rotatable Bond Features**:
   - f_rot = N_rotatable / N_heavy_bonds (fraction of rotatable bonds)
   - Backbone rotatable bonds vs side-chain rotatable bonds (different impact on Tg)
   - Dihedral barrier estimates: Use RDKit to estimate rotation barriers (sp³-sp³: ~3 kcal/mol, sp²-sp³: ~1 kcal/mol, sp²-sp² conjugated: ~10 kcal/mol)

2. **Steric Hindrance Index**:
   - For each backbone atom, compute van der Waals volume of side groups within 5Å
   - Sum over backbone: SHI = Σ V_side_chain(i) / N_backbone
   - High SHI = restricted rotation = high Tg

3. **Conjugation Extent**:
   - Identify conjugated paths (alternating single-double bonds, aromatic systems)
   - Compute: (a) Longest conjugated path length; (b) Total conjugated atoms; (c) Conjugation continuity (fraction of backbone that is conjugated)
   - High conjugation = rigid backbone = high Tg

4. **Backbone Stiffness Index**:
   - Identify ring systems in backbone (rigid) vs flexible linkers
   - Compute: BSI = (N_ring_atoms_backbone + N_conjugated_atoms_backbone) / N_backbone_atoms
   - Direct measure of backbone rigidity

5. **Persistence Length Proxy** (estimated from 2D):
   - Use empirical correlation: l_p ∝ BSI × (1 + SHI) / f_rot
   - Normalize by typical values for known polymers

**Stage 2: Rigidity→Tg Mapping**
Option A (Physics-informed): Use modified Flory-Fox equation:
   Tg = Tg_inf - K / M_n (modified to include rigidity features)
   Tg_pred = α + β₁×BSI + β₂×(1-f_rot) + β₃×SHI + β₄×Conjugation + γ×ECFP4

Option B (Data-driven): Train LightGBM on rigidity features + ECFP4

**Architecture Comparison:**
- CRIP-A: Rigidity features only (5-10 dims) → Linear regression
- CRIP-B: Rigidity features + ECFP4 → LightGBM
- CRIP-C: Rigidity features → MLP (2 layers, 32 hidden) → concatenate with ECFP4 → MLP

**Training:** 5-fold CV on Tg dataset. Target: CRIP-B < 33.0 RMSE.

**Interpretability Analysis:**
- Correlate each rigidity feature with Tg (expected: BSI↑→Tg↑, f_rot↑→Tg↓, SHI↑→Tg↑, Conjugation↑→Tg↑)
- Feature importance in LightGBM should reveal dominant rigidity factors
- Compare with ECFP4 feature importance - rigidity features should capture orthogonal information
Y: Y1: If H1 and H2 correct, rigidity features alone (CRIP-A) will achieve RMSE < 40.0, demonstrating that chain rigidity is the primary determinant of Tg and is predictable from structure.
Y2: If H3 correct, CRIP-B (rigidity + ECFP4) will outperform ECFP4 alone (38.78) by >3 RMSE, demonstrating that explicit rigidity features capture information missing in fingerprints.

Y3: Rigidity features will show strong correlations with Tg: (a) BSI correlation r > 0.6; (b) f_rot correlation r < -0.5; (c) SHI correlation r > 0.4. These correlations provide interpretable physics insights.

Y4: If H4 correct, analysis of PerioGT's learned representations (if accessible) should show high correlation with rigidity features, suggesting PerioGT implicitly learns rigidity through contrastive pre-training.

Y5: Two-stage model provides interpretability: for any polymer, we can explain 'This polymer has high Tg because it has BSI=0.8 (rigid backbone), f_rot=0.1 (few rotatable bonds), and SHI=2.5 (high steric hindrance).'

Y6: If CRIP fails to improve over ECFP4, this suggests either: (a) Tg is not primarily determined by chain rigidity (contradicting polymer physics); (b) Our rigidity features are insufficient; (c) The 8.19 RMSE gap comes from other factors (intermolecular interactions, morphology).

Y7: Success would establish a new paradigm: instead of black-box structure→property prediction, use interpretable structure→intermediate→property models that align with physical mechanisms. This approach could generalize to other polymer properties (Tm, modulus, etc.) with appropriate intermediate properties.

memory.abstract: This paper presents a foundation ML interatomic potential integrating equivariant graph neural networks with explicit polarizable long-range interactions via a core-shell charge equilibration scheme, demonstrating superior accuracy in capturing long-range electrostatics, polarization under external fields, and materials modeling across the periodic table.

content.background: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) based on equivariant graph neural networks (NequIP, MACE, etc.) have achieved excellent performance but typically use local cutoffs (~5Å) that fail to capture long-range phenomena. Message-passing mechanisms can extend effective cutoffs through layer-wise propagation, but become ineffective when graph connections break (e.g., molecules separated beyond cutoff distance). Long-range behaviors encompass electrostatic interactions between charged particles and dispersion terms from electron distribution fluctuations. Existing explicit long-range models (CENT, 4G-HDNNP, CELLI) typically train charge equilibration parameters to minimize differences between predicted and QM-derived partial charges. However, partial charges from QM calculations are ambiguous due to basis set incompleteness and partitioning method variances. The polarizable charge equilibration (PQEq) method addresses this by using QM electrostatic interaction energies rather than partial charges as targets, proving effective for capturing polarization effects through explicit core-shell displacement. This work addresses the fundamental question: can explicit polarizable long-range physics integrated with equivariant GNNs create a foundation model that captures phenomena inaccessible to local message-passing mechanisms?
content.method: The framework integrates equivariant message-passing neural networks with explicit polarizable long-range interactions. The total potential energy is decomposed as: E_pot = Σ_i E_0^i + E_PQEq + E_D3, where E_0^i is the neural network output for atom i, E_PQEq is the polarizable electrostatic energy, and E_D3 is the DFT-D3 dispersion correction. The core innovation is the polarizable charge equilibration scheme using a core-shell Gaussian model: each atom's partial charge q_i = q_ic + q_is (core + shell), with a harmonic spring constant K_s^i coupling core and shell positions. The energy includes electronegativity (χ^0) and chemical hardness (η^0) terms. The electrostatic energy uses Gaussian charge distributions with Coulomb interactions between all core-shell pairs. A self-consistent iterative procedure solves for partial charges and shell positions subject to charge conservation and chemical potential equality. The neural network component (NequIP architecture with 6 equivariant layers, 256 node features, 5Å cutoff) captures non-electrostatic energy contributions, ensuring no overlap with the explicit electrostatic treatment. Forces and stresses are computed via automatic differentiation. The foundation model was trained on MPtrj dataset covering the periodic table up to Pu, using PBE/PBE+U exchange-correlation with energy consistency corrections.
content.experiment: Validation proceeded in three phases. First, benchmark tests on charge-state datasets (C10H2/C10H3+, Na8/9Cl8+, Ag3+/-, Au2-MgO, BTA-Cu) comparing against 4G-HDNNP and NequIP. The framework achieved best results on most datasets (e.g., C10H2/C10H3+ energy MAE: 0.44 vs 1.19 meV/atom for 4G-HDNNP; Ag+ energy MAE: 4.87 vs 1.32 meV/atom for 4G-HDNNP, force MAE: 0.028 vs 0.032 eV/Å). Second, foundation model evaluation on MPtrj test set achieved 18 meV/atom energy MAE, 0.065 eV/Å force MAE, 0.301 GPa stress MAE. Critical validation included: (1) Na-Na/Na-Cl dimers at 1.8-12Å distances showing correct long-range behavior beyond the 5Å cutoff where message-passing fails; (2) water molecule polarization under external electric fields demonstrating correct response orthogonal to molecular dipole (QEq models show zero response); (3) bulk modulus prediction on 10,154 materials achieving R²=0.94. Third, application demonstrations: Li-ion diffusivity in c-LLZO solid electrolyte (2ns MD, 64 formula units) reproducing AIMD activation energies; BaTiO3 ferroelectric phase transitions (10×10×10 supercell) capturing rhombohedral→orthorhombic→tetragonal→cubic sequence; Li/Li3PS4 interface SEI formation (13,760 atoms, 4ns) revealing crystalline Li2S and amorphous Li3P formation. Computational efficiency: 0.07s per MD step for 2160 atoms (vs 0.91s for universal MLIPs), 1.49s for 24,000 atoms.
content.result: The explicit polarizable long-range framework significantly outperforms local MLIPs and charge-independent message-passing models across diverse charge-state systems. Key findings: (1) Long-range interactions beyond cutoff are correctly captured through explicit electrostatics, while message-passing models fail when graph connections break. (2) The core-shell model correctly reproduces polarization under external electric fields, addressing a fundamental limitation of QEq-based point-charge models. (3) The foundation model successfully balances accuracy and computational efficiency, enabling nanosecond-scale simulations of tens of thousands of atoms. (4) Transferability is demonstrated through accurate prediction of molecular polarizability (MAE 4.57 a.u. on QM-7b) and potential energy surfaces for neutral/ionic states. (5) Finetuning with 20% of target data achieves ab initio accuracy for specific systems. Limitations: The approach uses fixed PQEq parameters rather than learning them dynamically; higher-order charge expansion methods may achieve higher accuracy for complex systems at greater computational cost. Future directions include integration with complementary approaches (Latent Ewald Summation, LSR-MP, Neural P3M) and exploration of higher-order polarization terms.

It demonstrates that explicit long-range physics modules integrated with neural networks can capture phenomena that local message-passing mechanisms fundamentally miss: (1) interactions beyond cutoff distances (Na-Na/Na-Cl dimers), (2) polarization under external fields (water molecule), (3) layered material stability (LiFePO4). The core-shell charge equilibration approach offers a physics-grounded alternative to learned long-range representations. This directly addresses the ~1-3 RMSE gap estimated from missing long-range interactions in polymer Tg prediction.

(2) The decomposition E_total = E_NN + E_long-range + E_dispersion suggests a modular architecture where fingerprint-based local features are complemented by explicit physics-based long-range terms. (4) The finding that message-passing fails when graph connections break has implications for polymer multimer representation - disconnected chains require explicit long-range treatment. (5) Computational efficiency (0.07s/step for 2160 atoms) suggests the approach is practical for polymer property prediction datasets.

memory.abstract: Introduces polymer graph representation that adds periodic edge to trimer for capturing polymer periodicity, combined with MPNN for automatic feature learning. Achieves 20% average error reduction over molecular descriptors across 10 properties, and 34.91 RMSE on Tg prediction. Validates that monomer representations produce non-unique encodings and incorrect bonding environments for polymers.
memory.keyword: polymer graph, periodic representation, message passing neural network, learned descriptors, property prediction

content.background: Polymer informatics faces a fundamental representation challenge: existing methods use monomer-based representations transferred from molecular machine learning, but these fail to capture the periodic, extended structure of polymers. The authors identify three critical issues with monomer representations: (1) non-unique representations for polymers with identical monomers but different structures (e.g., polymers with same C-C-O repeat unit but different connectivity), (2) incorrect bonding environments where functional groups are artificially fragmented, and (3) lack of periodicity leading to inconsistent featurizations under trivial translations along the polymer backbone. Polymers consist of 10^0-10^6 repeating units, fundamentally different from finite molecules. This work addresses the grand challenge of developing polymer-specific representations that encode periodicity without requiring hand-crafted features.
content.method: The core innovation is the polymer graph representation: starting from a trimer graph (three repeat units), an additional edge is added connecting the two terminal atoms, creating a periodic structure. This approach is analogous to crystal graph representations for 3D periodic materials, where the unit cell interacts with periodic copies. The periodic edge serves two purposes: (1) maintaining correct bonding environment for all atoms (no artificially cleaved bonds), and (2) enabling message passing throughout the polymer chain. The graph is processed by a Message Passing Neural Network (MPNN) implemented in Chemprop, using directed bond-level messages with 300-dimensional message vectors, 3 message-passing steps, and a 2-layer feed-forward network (300 hidden units each). The learned polymer encoding from the final hidden layer serves as an automatically optimized descriptor for property prediction. The representation naturally handles polymers that share monomers but have different connectivity patterns.
content.experiment: Dataset: 15,219 data points across 10 polymer properties from PolyInfo (experimental Tg, density) and DFT calculations (atomization energy, crystallization tendency, band gap chain/bulk, electron affinity, ionization energy, refractive index, dielectric constant), spanning 9,935 unique homopolymers. Baselines: Random Forest with 200 RDKit molecular descriptors (115 chemical characteristics + 85 binary fragment features), MPNN with monomer graph. Ablation studies compared polymer graph vs trimer graph (no periodic edge) vs dimer graph vs monomer graph. A targeted experiment tested 179 Tg polymers where each polymer has at least one other with identical monomer representation. Feature analysis correlated MPNN-learned features with known molecular descriptors to interpret what chemical information the model captures.
content.result: Main findings: (1) Polymer graph + MPNN achieves 20% average error reduction vs RF/molecular descriptors, and 10% vs monomer graph + MPNN. (2) On Tg prediction: polymer graph achieves 34.91 RMSE (vs RF 41.39, monomer graph 38.79). (3) For polymers with identical monomers, polymer graph achieves 39°C RMSE vs monomer graph's 49°C - monomer graphs predict identical values for different polymers, causing large errors. (4) Ablation: periodic edge contributes 4% average improvement (32% for atomization energy); dimer and trimer graphs perform similarly (no additional chemical info beyond dimer). (5) RF with MPNN-learned descriptors achieves comparable performance to full MPNN (35.34 vs 34.91 RMSE on Tg), indicating learned representations - not architecture - drive improvement. (6) Learned features correlate with known Tg-relevant features: polar groups (NH, OH) and ring structures. Limitations: polymer graph still 4 RMSE above PerioGT SOTA (30.8), suggesting additional mechanisms needed. The approach handles 1D periodicity but does not address long-range entanglement interactions.
content.dataset: PolyInfo database (experimental Tg, density) + DFT calculations from prior work (atomization energy, crystallization tendency, band gap chain/bulk, electron affinity, ionization energy, refractive index, dielectric constant); 15,219 total data points across 9,935 unique homopolymers
content.topic_relation: Directly addresses Graph_Transformer_for_Global_Topology hypothesis (Rank 2) by providing evidence that periodicity encoding improves polymer prediction. Validates that simple graph topology modifications (periodic edge) provide measurable but limited improvement (+4% average, +0.29 RMSE in FP-PGNN experiment). The 34.91 RMSE on Tg vs PerioGT's 30.8 suggests PerioGT has additional mechanisms beyond periodicity encoding. Confirms fingerprint+learned features are competitive with end-to-end GNN. Supports Long_Short_Range_Message_Passing hypothesis (Rank 1) - the gap between polymer graph and SOTA may require long-range interaction modeling.
content.topic_contribution: Provides validated baseline: polymer graph + MPNN achieves 34.91 RMSE on Tg, establishing that periodicity-aware representation alone is insufficient to reach SOTA (30.8). The learned descriptor analysis confirms MPNNs extract chemically meaningful features (polar groups, ring structures) relevant to Tg. The non-unique representation problem demonstrates why monomer graphs fail - critical for understanding PerioGT's mechanism. Enables decision: focus on long-range interactions (LSR-MP style) rather than further periodicity encoding refinements, as periodic edge contribution is limited. Suggests investigating what additional mechanisms PerioGT uses beyond periodicity-aware attention.

memory.abstract: Ewald message passing augments MPNNs with a Fourier-space scheme using frequency cutoffs instead of distance cutoffs to capture long-range interactions (electrostatics, van der Waals), achieving 10-16% energy MAE improvement on OC20 and OE62 datasets across four baseline models, with outsize impact on structures with high long-range energy contributions.
memory.keyword: long-range interactions, Ewald summation, message passing neural networks, Fourier space filtering, periodic systems

content.background: Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) have become the dominant paradigm for learning molecular potential energy surfaces, achieving orders of magnitude speedup over quantum chemistry methods. However, MPNNs rely on spatial distance cutoffs for computational efficiency, which fundamentally limits their ability to capture long-range interactions such as electrostatics and van der Waals forces. This limitation is particularly severe for periodic materials where interatomic distances are unbounded. In molecular dynamics, non-bonded energy terms (electrostatics, dispersion) exhibit power-law decay with distance, making simple truncation artifacts-prone even at large cutoffs. The Ewald summation method from computational physics addresses this by decomposing interactions into short-range (distance-truncated) and long-range (frequency-truncated in Fourier space) components. This paper bridges Ewald summation and GNN architectures, proposing Ewald message passing as a general framework to complement existing MPNN layers.
content.method: Ewald message passing is built on a formal analogy between continuous-filter convolutions and electrostatic interactions. In standard MPNNs, message sums M_i = Σ_j h_j · Φ(||x_i - x_j||) aggregate neighbor information using learned radial filters Φ. This is analogous to computing electrostatic potentials V_i = Σ_j q_j / ||x_i - x_j||. The key insight is that Ewald summation decomposes a long-ranged kernel Φ into short-range Φ^sr (fast distance decay, distance-truncated) and long-range Φ^lr (well-defined at origin, fast frequency decay). The long-range component is computed in Fourier space: M^lr(x_i) = Σ_k exp(ik^T x_i) · s_k · Φ^lr(||k||), where s_k = Σ_j h_j exp(-ik^T x_j) are structure factor embeddings. This enables a frequency cutoff c_k instead of distance cutoff c_x. The method has three steps: (1) compute structure factor embeddings via Fourier sum over atoms, (2) multiply k-wise with learned filter values, (3) inverse Fourier sum scatters messages back to atoms. For periodic systems, frequencies are discretized by the reciprocal lattice. For aperiodic systems, a voxel grid discretization is used with rotation-invariant coordinate frames. The computational complexity is O(N_at · N_k), and sub-quadratic scaling is achievable by fixing N_k. Ewald MP is integrated by adding long-range messages to standard MPNN updates via skip connections.
content.experiment: The method was tested on two datasets: OC20 (periodic adsorption energies, 265M structures, trained on OC20-2M subsplit) and OE62 (aperiodic organic molecules, 62K structures with DFT-D3 dispersion corrections). Four baseline models were modified: SchNet, PaiNN, DimeNet++, and GemNet-T. Integration was minimal: long-range messages were added via skip connections during each interaction block. For aperiodic OE62, radial basis filtering with frequency cutoff c_k was used; for periodic OC20, fixed numbers of reciprocal lattice frequencies (N_x, N_y, N_z) were used. Comparison studies included: (1) increased distance cutoff c_x and neighbor threshold N_max, (2) replacing Ewald block with SchNet block with increased cutoff, (3) matching parameter count via larger embeddings. Results showed consistent improvements across all models: average 16.1% on OE62 and 10.3% on OC20. Ewald MP achieved better cost-performance tradeoff than large cutoff settings. Ablation on OE62 binned by DFT-D3 correction magnitude revealed outsize improvements for structures with high long-range contributions, confirming the method targets long-range interactions.
content.result: Ewald MP provides robust energy MAE improvements (10-16%) across diverse models and datasets with minimal architectural changes. Key findings: (1) The method recovers effects of DFT-D3 dispersion correction without hand-crafting, matching or surpassing a 'cheating' baseline that explicitly adds D3 ground truth. (2) Improvements are more pronounced for structures with high long-range energy contributions, validating the mechanism. (3) Force MAE improvements on OC20 are small but consistent, expected since frequency truncation removes high-frequency contributions affecting gradients. (4) The approach is more efficient on periodic structures (OC20) at half the relative cost. (5) Integration is cheaper alongside models with few but compute-heavy blocks (DimeNet++, GemNet-T). Limitations: The frequency truncation scheme removes fine-grained resolution below scale ~c_k^-1, limiting impact on energy gradients (forces). Future work includes adapting more efficient Ewald variants (FFT-based) for sub-quadratic scaling.
content.dataset: OC20 (periodic adsorption energies, 265M structures), OE62 (aperiodic organic molecules, 62K structures)
content.topic_relation: Directly supports Long_Short_Range_Message_Passing hypothesis (Rank 1). Provides evidential support: (1) 10-16% improvement via explicit long-range modules, (2) Fourier-space scheme captures long-range interactions that distance-cutoff MPNNs miss, (3) particularly effective for structures with high long-range contributions. The paper validates that long-range interactions are a significant missing component in standard MPNNs. Also relevant to polymer prediction: polymer physics involves chain entanglement interactions at 10-100+ atom distances, analogous to the long-range electrostatics/dispersion captured by Ewald MP.
content.topic_contribution: Actionable: Implement Ewald-style Fourier-space message passing for polymer Tg prediction. The structure factor embedding approach can capture chain entanglement effects that extend beyond local covalent bonds. For polymers: (1) Adapt the aperiodic case discretization (voxel grid) since polymer repeat units are not periodic in 3D, (2) The frequency cutoff mechanism may capture the multi-scale nature of polymer chain interactions, (3) Test whether structures with high long-range contributions (e.g., highly entangled polymers) show larger improvements. The ~1-3 RMSE gap attributed to long-range interactions in Day 3 analysis could potentially be recovered through this mechanism. Decision enabled: Design LEMP (Long-range Entanglement-aware Message Passing) experiment with Ewald-style Fourier filtering adapted for 1D polymer chains.
